title: Adversarial Speculative Reasoning Improves Long Horizon Agents
summary: Speculative decoding has been treated purely as a systems optimization that speeds up large language model decoding without changing the model behavior. Under this view, the growing effort to train better draft models has been focused solely on acceptance rate. We argue that this view does not hold true for long-horizon agent reasoning. Measuring frontier open-weight models on complex agentic tasks with different speculative decoding approaches, we found that numerical noise grows within verification windows, and the draft acceptance results of the thinking process can change the output distribution of the model after 30 steps, thus noticeably influencing the reasoning accuracy of long-horizon agents in random directions. In this work, we improve the reasoning capability of target models by controlling such noise. While we cannot change the overall token distribution verified by the target model, we can encode critical reasoning with highest precision by training the draft model to be rejected. We identify these points in agent traces and train the draft model to favor adversarial preference. At inference the trained draft and the target part ways precisely at these decision points, verification restarts, so that critical thinking tokens are sampled from the target model and encoded under its least noisy conditions. This approach makes critical reasoning better indexed and more durable over a long horizon. On complex agentic coding benchmarks, our approach raises end-to-end success rate with no change to the target model or its output distribution. Our results recast the speculative decoding mechanism from a pure accelerator into an active allocator for context precision that improves the accuracy of long-horizon agents by training 0.06% to 0.28% of hosted parameters.

title: HARP: Training-Free Dual-Profile Agentic Communication for LLM-Based Recommendation
summary: In LLM-based recommendation, memory acts as a user-level agent in a memory-augmented backbone. Yet users and items remain asymmetric: only the user is given a structured profile; it enters a bandwidth-limited reranker prompt; and it is frozen after warmup. We recast LLM-based recommendation as an agentic-communication process in four stages: BUILD a self-description, TRANSMIT it along the collaborative graph, UNDERSTAND the other side, and SYNC it from the next interaction. This formulation reveals three unresolved communication challenges: the item side never produces a comparable self-description (one-sided BUILD); profile-level signals enter only the bandwidth-limited reranker prompt rather than retrieval, where they would not compete for context tokens (prompt-trapped UNDERSTAND); and the user's description is frozen after warmup with no principled update rule (absent SYNC). We instantiate the missing stages as HARP (Homophily-aware Agentic Recommendation via dual Profiles), a training-free, three-operator addition to a frozen LLM backbone: a rule-extracted symmetric item profile (zero extra LLM calls), a channel-decomposable profile-level homophily H(phi_u, phi_i) consumed at retrieval time rather than inside the reranker prompt, and a single-pass reflective update realising in-context profile evolution without any gradient step. On four public benchmarks (Yelp, Books, MovieTV, Goodreads), HARP lifts Hit@1 over the strongest published baseline by 6.9%-24.0%, with family-wise Holm-corrected p < 1e-9 on every dataset. Ablations and a per-case attribution study show that the operators contribute complementary gains, with the retrieval-side gate as the main source; we also report the trade-off introduced by the reflective pass. We formulate agentic communication and provide a training-free instantiation. Code is available at https://github.com/Jove-Zhen/HARP.

title: Where Is the Truth When AI Agents Disagree? Dependence-Aware Belief Propagation for Unsupervised Truth Discovery (Extended Version)
summary: LLM agents often give conflicting answers to the same question, and many deployed agents are variants of one base model, so their errors are correlated. We study truth discovery among such agents: inferring the true answer and each agent's reliability without labels. Classical truth-discovery and crowdsourcing estimators reward an agreeing bloc and can fall below majority vote. We propose BP-TD, which adds per-agent decorrelation weights to mean-field variational inference on a one-coin Dawid-Skene model, so that agents sharing a base model count together as about one vote. Its first iteration is exactly a weighted vote; later iterations estimate agent reliability. With 13 local agents on MMLU, BP-TD beats majority vote without any labels (0.716 vs. 0.624 on 160 questions; 0.707 vs. 0.674 on 10,000) and ranks agents by their true accuracy, which classical estimators invert. The gain depends on the pool: over 2,852 sub-pools of four benchmarks, decorrelation helps when the largest correlated bloc is weaker than the other agents and hurts when it is the strongest, and we found no label-free statistic that tells the two cases apart. Labels change the picture quickly: with 20 labelled questions, selecting the single best agent is more accurate than every aggregator we tested on MMLU, ARC and TruthfulQA.

title: [AINews] LLMs can read & write neural network weights: "Weight Space Programming" cuts Autoresearch out of the RSI loop
summary: Editing Qwen’s weights to reduce reasoning loops, DeepSeek’s super-agent prototype, and the GDPx benchmark.

content_excerpt: Keyword matches words; semantic matches meaning and exact titles or names; hybrid combines both. In keyword mode, use quotation marks for exact phrases. Author matches published credits. Year applies to posts; wiki entries have no author or publication year. You can also use author:"Ada" or type:podcast in non-regex searches. Editing Qwen’s weights to reduce reasoning loops, DeepSeek’s super-agent prototype, and the GDPx benchmark. Amid a deepening bear market for AI/tech (worthy of dark humor ) with Anthropic bonds receiving a “junk” rating and OpenAI fundraise headlines , we continue to see very surprising capability finds in the community, such as today. The best way to put today’s blockbuster paper in context is to recall Karpathy’s autoresearch from a mere 8 months ago , which presaged a summer of recursive self improvement fears : Abstractly, the demonstration is that you can take a sufficiently smart model and through running a series of experiments across a compute cluster, train a model autonomously without human expertise or intervention. However, this is usually done by an involved process of writing PyTorch/Jax code and running compute and watching loss curves and reading evals and optimizing kernels and data and…. Well, last month’s guest Alex Zhang comes back to coauthor a MONSTER discovery: what if you just ask a smart model to directly read and edit the weights of a dumber model? In ML this is the equivalent of not looking at source code, just directly seeing the 1’s and 0’s of ( very small ) compiled executables, and being able to 1) tell what they do , 2) oneshot-fix bugs given failed traces or, with 50 steps, improve in a general direction ( possible overstatement here ), 3) writing entire network weights from scratch in one shot , beating some independently trained models. If you believe that LLMs can truly fit and simulate everything given enough parameters (and in fact, LLMs are increasingly better calculators as you grow in size), then something like this was in theory bound to happen, but it is surprising nevertheless to have the ability suddenly emerge, as an independent reproduction seems to already have found: Of course the exact thing we are really modeling is some variant of mechanistic interpretability (which could be done by hand ), and right now unlikely to scale to more advanced tasks than simple games and RL policies, but the world has now gone from 0 to 1 on this very new RSI capability…. which will immediately put to use

title: Maggie Appleton: Agentic Coding Has Outgrown the Text Box
summary:
Agentic coding has outgrown the text box. Maggie Appleton, staff research engineer at GitHub Next, argues that walls of CLI output and AGENTS.md files serve coding agents far better than the humans steering them. She walks through Chopin, the GitHub Next prototype where background agents turn a team's planning chat into a structured plan, and makes the case for agents that prompt you instead of waiting to be prompted.

What we cover:
– Why text-heavy agentic coding tools favor agents over humans
– Boundary objects: what AGENTS.md, skill files and MCP servers get right and wrong
– Multiplayer planning with coding agents in GitHub Next's Chopin
– Human-to-agent handoffs, formal verification and spec-driven development
– Why software quality is rising, not falling, with coding agents
– Which roles still matter: PMs, designers and engineers

title: Why Agents Are Soon Only Going to Have 1 Tool
summary: Instead of triggering tools one at a time across turns, agents are collapsing their tool catalog into a single exec(code) tool—chaining, filtering, and awaiting actions inside an isolated sandbox.
story_key: story|title:why agents are soon only going to have 1 tool
content_excerpt: For the past two years, building capable Agents meant designing tools, figuring out which actions help the model complete a task, deciding how granular each tool schema needs to be, or iterating on system instruction templates. This is changing. Agents are moving in the opposite direction by collapsing their entire tool catalog into one tool : exec . This is called Code Mode (or Programmatic Tool Calling). Instead of forcing the model to trigger tools one at a time across turns, the harness gives the model a single exec(code) tool. The model writes a short TypeScript or Python script that chains, combines, and awaits actions inside an isolated sandbox. To understand why agents are converging on a single exec tool, we should look at how tool calling evolved. Initially, we only gave agents a handful of tools because they couldn't reliably choose or filter across a large catalog. As models improved, we connected dozens of tools or MCP servers, but ran into context window limits. We solved that with tool search and progressive disclosure , letting agents look up tools on demand. Even with dynamic tool loading, we still had dozens of individual tools, and were still stuck with the limitation of standard tool calling: one action per turn. In standard tool calling, the model generates a structured object (typically JSON) that defines a single action (or at best a flat batch of independent calls, like reading three files), waits for the raw output to come back, adds it into the prompt history, reasons again, and decides what to do next. From my own experience, we made a big jump recently in how reliably models can combine and chain dependent actions in a single pass: Several shifts came together to enable this. Frontier models are trained heavily on code, and providers have started post-training models for Code Mode. At the same time, MCP servers now increasingly ship outputSchema alongside inputSchema , giving the model upfront knowledge of return types so it can chain Tool A into Tool B inside the same script before seeing runtime output. Code Mode collapses the tool catalog into a single tool on the model surface: exec(code) . Instead of passing 80 separate JSON Schema tool objects to the model API, the agent compiles those schemas into compact type declarations ( declare namespace tools { ... } ). title: GDPx: Measuring Frontier Model Capabilities Across the Most Valuable Domains
summary: A frontier benchmark spanning RSI, hardware design, cyber, bio, finance, legal, quant trading, chip design, software engineering, materials science, and alignment
story_key: story|title:gdpx measuring frontier model capabilities across the most valuable domains
content_excerpt: GDPx is a benchmark that covers the most valuable domains for frontier intelligence. It aims to be the world’s best benchmark for measuring general agentic capabilities. We believe the first trillion dollars of AI revenue will be concentrated in sectors that can deploy frontier intelligence at high ROI , not broadly diffused throughout the whole economy. Building a general-purpose benchmark based on share of GDP or the SOC/O*NET occupational taxonomy is therefore a mistake. If your goal is to track the progress of frontier models, you should focus on the domains where they will be most impactful. It’s worth emphasizing that certain models like Opus 5.5 and GPT-6 Astra have sandbagged overall scores due to their safety classifiers. If we exclude cyber, biology, and alignment—the three domains where safety classifiers sometimes kick in—you get the following results instead. We were pleasantly surprised by how well this ranking lines up with our subjective impression of the models. OpenAI and Anthropic generally dominate the top of the ranking while SpaceXAI, Meta, and open-weight models are all meaningfully behind. Gemini 4 Carbon is a real improvement from Google and the only model in the same ballpark as Opus and Astra. It will be interesting to see people’s impressions once Carbon becomes generally available. We believe it’s underrated how relevant safety classifiers are when picking the best model for certain use cases. For example, Muse Wonder Full is actually the best available cyber model today by a meaningful margin . Opus 5.5 is the best all-around model and wins in quant trading, hardware design, and chip design. Gemini 4 Carbon is the best bio model (likely due to weaker safety classifiers) and edges out the win in software engineering. GPT-6 Astra wins convincingly for RSI and is also the best model for materials science. Our finance and legal tasks are so challenging that basically every model scores exactly 0. Interestingly, if you subset to a single model family, you will sometimes see very similar spikes. The cost vs performance Pareto frontier also matches our general experience using the models: Luna and DeepSeek fight for the low end, Opus wins the high end, and OpenAI claims the middle. Again, however, the appearance of Gemini 4 Carbon is worth watching closely. It’s impossible to make all the nuanced comparisons enabled by GDPx in a single newsletter. title: Who is the Pronoun Pro? Comparing LLMs and Humans at Number-Disambiguation of 'they'
summary: This study evaluates whether large language models (LLMs) can reliably replace or complement human research assistants in linguistically complex annotation. In a controlled annotation task, 73 human annotators (local students and crowdworkers with and without a background in linguistics) and more than 40 LLM configurations number-disambiguated 174 authentic uses of 'they' from Reddit, including innovative and context-sensitive cases. The best LLM, Kimi K3, reached 94.5% accuracy, above the human majority vote (86.2%) and the mean of the top half of human annotators (78.5%); only the single best human annotator scored higher (95.7%). LLMs also offer substantial practical advantages in cost and speed. However, qualitative error analysis reveals a crucial complementarity: human reasoning in low-agreement cases exposes inconsistencies in the annotation typology and thereby improves the methodological framework itself. The study contributes (i) a benchmark-style human-LLM comparison for a semantically demanding task, (ii) transparent cost and time evidence, and (iii) a methodological argument against a purely replacement-oriented view of automation. LLMs are viable for large-scale annotation support in linguistics, but their responsible use requires human critical oversight. The dataset with its gold-standard labels, all human and LLM annotations, and the fully reproducible code are openly available as a Quarto-based, public repository.

title: JHiMA-WebRL: A Joint Hierarchical Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning Framework for Long-Horizon Web Tasks
summary: Multimodal web agents have shown promising capabilities for interacting with websites through graphical user interfaces (GUIs), yet realistic web tasks often require long-horizon, multi-step planning that remains challenging for monolithic policies. Such agents must jointly infer high-level plans, navigate through intermediate states, track progress over extended interaction histories, and execute visually grounded actions. Although prior work has explored modular multi-agent systems with a separate planner, the planner is typically not updated jointly with the actor. We investigate whether explicitly separating and jointly training planning and execution provides a stronger inductive bias for long-horizon web navigation. We introduce JHiMA-WebRL, a joint hierarchical multi-agent reinforcement learning framework for web agents that couples a task decomposer with an actor. To train the decomposer, we use a strong teacher model to construct structured subtask supervision from multimodal GUI trajectories, and use these annotations to fine-tune both the decomposer and the subtask-conditioned actor. We then extend Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) to jointly optimize the decomposer and actor in the interactive WebArena environment through hierarchical rollout grouping and role-specific advantages. On WebArena-Lite-v2, JHiMA-WebRL-14B, consisting of a 7B actor and a 7B decomposer, achieves an average success rate of 37.2%, compared with 24% for a ScaleCUA-32B agent that we fine-tune with RL on the same training tasks and evaluate under the same protocol. Ablations show that jointly updating the decomposer during RL outperforms updating the actor alone. These results suggest that jointly learned role factorization with smaller models can be a competitive alternative to scaling monolithic agents for long-horizon web tasks.

title: claude-code v2.1.317
summary:
What's changed

  • Added a warning to /schedule when a new cloud scheduled task gets connectors you did not ask for, with how to remove them
  • Added a check that asks before a web or shell tool call sends your account email address to the network
  • Added onFailure: "block" for Agent SDK hook callbacks, so a callback that fails blocks the action instead of letting it run
  • Added a notice in Claude Desktop's Code tab when your organization's remote managed settings haven't loaded for the session, and another once they do
  • Added a notice when auto mode's check has no answer for a subagent's tool call, which used to leave nothing in the main view
  • Added anthropic.plan, anthropic.seat_type, anthropic.provider and anthropic.custom_base_url to OTel metrics, events and spans
  • Added a cost report to the Claude apps gateway admin API, GET /v1/organizations/analytics/cost, for reading past spend over a date range in total, per developer, per day or per IdP group
  • Added a daily record of each developer's IdP groups on Claude apps gateways with admin: set, kept for admin.identity_retention_days, which the cost report groups by
  • Added CLAUDE_CODE_DISABLE_NESTED_SESSION_ID: set it to 1 on a self-hosted runner to have claude -p run inside a session use that session's ID and transcript, as in earlier versions
  • Fixed project and local MCP servers disconnecting after the first turn in some Claude desktop sessions
  • Fixed auto mode failing every turn when an LLM gateway set as the base URL answers 403 or 422 to its server-side safety check (a 403 with an apiKeyHelper is unchanged)
  • Fixed claude auth status exiting before a slow token refresh was saved, which could sign you out on the next run
  • Fixed a project's effortLevel setting being ignored by sessions that an app starts ahead of time and then opens in the project, such as new sessions in the desktop app's Code tab
  • Fixed claude --from-pr reporting "No conversations found" in projects with many sessions when the linked session was older than the first page
  • Fixed the second of two simultaneous permission prompts showing no file path or command on claude.ai and the mobile apps
  • Fixed Remote Control and SDK hosts offering "don't ask again" on a mod's tool calls
  • Fixed session titles being lost in cloud and SDK sessions when a new message or Stop arrived while the title was generating
  • Fixed self-paced /loop wakeups sometimes not being scheduled when Claude left a field out of its request
  • Fixed auto mode in cloud sessions stopping for approval when the Artifact tool uploaded, wrote to a database or saved a file through the outputs folder
  • Fixed skills synced from claude.ai being lost or downloaded again every ten minutes when they can't be written to disk
  • Fixed /schedule leaving a cloud scheduled task's next run time and link out of its results after creating or updating it
  • Fixed screen readers speaking a running subagent's elapsed time and token count on every change in screen reader mode
  • Fixed a region or network block (HTTP 403) being shown as a sign-in failure; the error now explains the block
  • Fixed Claude saying a working claude.ai connector needed authorization or had failed in cloud sessions when a synced plugin included the same server
  • Fixed claude -p exiting 0 when a full disk or quota lost its transcript or ~/.claude.json writes; it now prints an error and, in text and json output, exits 1. Full NFS exports may be missed
  • Fixed edits to settings files made in the first second or so after launch not taking effect until a settings file changed again
  • Fixed old transcripts not being cleaned up on machines where some runs skip cleanup, such as runs using --setting-sources
  • Fixed deleted agent team inboxes being re-created by a teammate's late message
  • Fixed a re-created agent teammate being removed from its team by an earlier shutdown approval
  • Fixed stored scheduled tasks being impossible to list or delete after scheduled tasks were turned off
  • Fixed Claude deleting your most recently updated /team-onboarding guide when asked to delete one without naming which
  • Fixed Claude saying a /team-onboarding guide was deleted when the server refused the delete
  • Fixed the Claude apps gateway hiding Amazon Bedrock's "Input is too long." error, which left sessions failing every turn with "upstream rejected the request" instead of compacting
  • Fixed self-hosted runner sessions losing recent turns or the whole conversation when restarted while a plan waited for approval
  • Fixed "Prompt is too long" after automatic compaction in sessions whose very large CLAUDE.md changed since it was last sent
  • Fixed high memory use and slow startup in headless sessions with many plugins that register commands
  • Fixed stdio MCP servers receiving an empty AWS_BEARER_TOKEN_BEDROCK when their env config sets it to empty; the variable is now unset, so the server can use the machine's own AWS credentials
  • Fixed API requests failing with "unable to get local issuer certificate" behind some TLS-inspecting proxies after a root certificate renewal
  • Fixed very long conversations losing their earlier summary when compaction had to shorten its own request
  • Fixed a PDF's own metadata being able to make Read and @-mentions under-count its pages
  • Fixed DISABLE_PROMPT_CACHING_OPUS and DISABLE_PROMPT_CACHING_SONNET having no effect on [1m], other-region and undated spellings of the default model
  • Fixed /artifacts and the Artifact tool's shared list showing no shared artifacts when you have 200 or more of your own
  • Fixed Claude treating partial Grep and Glob results as complete when a search hit its time limit
  • Fixed OpenTelemetry exports to an https:// endpoint through a proxy never being sent when they started while another export was still in progress
  • Fixed a flood of connection attempts to a proxy that blocks (HTTP 403) OpenTelemetry exports to an http:// endpoint
  • Fixed OpenTelemetry exports hanging indefinitely behind a proxy that never answers; they now time out after 10 seconds, or OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_TIMEOUT up to 30 seconds
  • Fixed resumed sessions telling Claude again about a file change it already knew about
  • Fixed Claude sometimes not using a built-in tool in a resumed session after an earlier call failed because the tool was switched off
  • Fixed /remote-control answering "Unknown command" instead of saying that Remote Control is turned off by the disableRemoteControl setting
  • Fixed agent team teammates in tmux or iTerm2 panes starting in auto mode when the lead session was in manual mode
  • Fixed a background session sometimes losing a just-made change of permission mode when it was upgraded or retired
  • Fixed Ctrl+C stopping all running background agents when pressed to clear typed text at the prompt
  • Fixed /feedback showing "Enter to confirm" while a report is being sent
  • Fixed child processes of a stopped shell command sometimes being sent SIGTERM twice, which could make some programs skip their cleanup

  • Improved the error shown on Microsoft Foundry when Azure credentials can't be loaded: it now says to check or refresh them, and reports as cloud_credential_error
  • Improved /design-sync to say up front when your design system has moved to Claude, and stop before building instead of failing at upload

  • Improved the "Resume this session with" hint shown at exit to repeat the flags you launched with (for example --chrome --debug) ahead of --resume

  • Changed exit to skip the "Background work is running" prompt for plugin monitors
  • Changed the built-in plugin-authoring skill to offer once, after a mod you built works, to help share the mod
  • Removed the Read tool's "file unchanged since your last Read" stub: reading an unchanged file again returns its content
  • Windows: Fixed every tool call being refused on some volumes where the native path lookup fails; the working-directory check now compares the folder's identity instead
  • Windows: Fixed the session scratchpad and other temporary paths growing with your project's path length in sessions not started by Claude Desktop, which made repositories cloned into them hit the 260-character path limit
  • Gateway: Fixed the status line and /usage showing a developer's own spend limit as 100% used after their group's pooled budget ran out
  • Self-hosted runner: Fixed Claude not seeing the interrupted tool call when a session moves to a new runner and the turn is older than CLAUDE_CODE_RESUME_INTERRUPTED_TURN_MAX_AGE_MS
  • Self-hosted runner: Fixed an MCP server that was switched off coming back on after the session moved to a new machine, when the session service had refused to save the switch
  • Remote Control: Improved fork names when the app doesn't set one: a long name keeps its "(fork)" ending, and in sessions started with claude remote-control a fork of "Name (fork)" is "Name (fork 2)"
  • [VSCode] Fixed forked conversations dropping messages: only one of the tool calls Claude ran in parallel was kept, and the last messages a compaction kept were lost, which could leave Claude's answer without the question it answered
  • [VSCode] Fixed a message being lost when Claude did not finish starting in time: the extension now starts Claude once more before showing the error
  • [VSCode] Fixed the sign-in screen opening when a request is blocked for its region or network
  • [VSCode] Fixed the Account panel showing the plan name with a lower-cased second word
  • [VSCode] Fixed file links in a Claude tab opening on top of the chat instead of in another editor group
  • [VSCode] Fixed attachment chips, menus, banners and dialogs in the Claude panel staying small when chat.fontSize is raised
  • [VSCode] Fixed ultrathink not raising effort for its turn or showing its rainbow when telemetry is off
  • [Cloud sessions] Added a link card to cloud sessions, so you can open or decline a link an MCP server asks you to visit instead of the request going unseen
  • [Cloud sessions] Changed the organization environment dialog in admin settings to the personal dialogs' short layout: each section opens from a row, and unsaved input asks before closing
  • [Cloud sessions] Fixed adding a network secret for a host that already has one silently replacing it; the Add secret form now refuses and points you to the existing secret
  • [Cloud sessions] Fixed new scheduled tasks ignoring your organization's default environment: the form now starts on the one an admin chose instead of the Anthropic-hosted default
  • [Remote Control] Fixed the next message to an idle session going unanswered after you restart claude remote-control, when you sent it within a minute of your previous message
  • [Claude Tag] Changed newly pasted artifact links in Slack to show a simpler card with an Open button that opens the artifact in Claude, instead of Slack's side panel
